title: Óc Eo – Ba Thế, the State Party of Viet Nam's own account of the site: Roman gold coins and medals, Han bronze mirrors and Persian lamps in one sentence
language_note: English, and it is the State Party of Viet Nam's English rather than an international body's. The submission's phrasing is left exactly as filed — `copper Roman gold coins and medals`, `turning goods through the sea trade route into a spearhead economy`, the ellipses that end several of its lists. UNESCO's own disclaimer says why that matters: `The sole responsibility for the content of each Tentative List lies with the State Party concerned.` This is Viet Nam describing Óc Eo, published by UNESCO, and the record treats it as the former.
date: The submission dates the culture `from the 2nd – 1st centuries BC to the "Oc Eo post-stage” about 8th-9th century AD`, which sits inside this project's window at both ends. Date of Submission of the tentative list itself: 04/01/2022. Ref. 6572, criteria (ii)(iii)(v), submitted by the Vietnamese National Commission for UNESCO.
findspot: `An Giang province, Thoai Son district`, as the submission's own header states it, in Oc Eo town, in the Mekong Delta of southern Viet Nam. The page also prints coordinates — `N100 15 24 E105 08 36`, with the degrees field evidently mistyped — AND THIS RECORD DOES NOT TAKE THEM. A coordinate reaches this corpus through a gazetteer id or not at all, and a coordinate a source hands over is refused exactly as the Scandinavian ones and `seasia-08-pong-tuk-lamp`'s were. The mistyped latitude is a second reason and not the reason.

original_text_excerpt: With wooden stilts, beams, railings, etc, collected along with many traces of decomposing wood in the Oc Eo field, it has clearly demonstrated the traditionally residential form of the ancient Oc Eo inhabitants who mainly settled on wooden stilts around the high mounds at the foot of the mountain. They have dug and filled many canals to exploit the cropland according to the seasons. On the high mounds, mountain slopes often have religious architectures, residences of clergy and nobles made of bricks, stones, wood, etc. They travel by boat, raft, canoe along canals or to the sea, carrying necessary items for river life such as cooking stove, pottery drinking bottles, fishing nets... International trade has been proven through artifacts found such as wooden boat pieces, copper Roman gold coins and medals, Han bronze mirrors, Persian lamps; glass materials, precious metals imported from India and Mediterranean countries further clarify the capacity of sea exploitation, turning goods through the sea trade route into a spearhead economy in the developing process of the ancient town of Oc Eo.
original_text_note:
ONE PARAGRAPH OF THE SUBMISSION'S `Criterion (v)` SECTION, WHOLE AND UNCUT, AND NOTHING IS ASSEMBLED. It is the forty-ninth paragraph of the rendered page, taken between paragraph boundaries rather than between phrases, so that no editorial choice about where to start and stop is being made inside a sentence. The paragraph was chosen because it is the one that carries the trade sentence; it is quoted entire rather than trimmed to that sentence, because a list of imports without the stilt houses, the canals and the boats around it is the corpus deciding what the State Party's argument was.

citation_original:
TWO POSITIONS ARE STATED AND THE PAGE DOES NOT SETTLE WHICH ONE COVERS THIS TEXT. The position is `two_positions_stated`.

FIRST, a blanket restriction. From https://whc.unesco.org/en/disclaimer/, read 2026-09-06:

"All photographs and other elements of the UNESCO World Heritage Centre website are protected by international treaties on intellectual property and other applicable laws. The elements it displays may not be copied or retransmitted by any means without explicit authorisation from the World Heritage Centre or the copyright holders."

SECOND, an open licence, on the same page, in a table headed `Intellectual Property | License source | License / Read Usage Terms`. Its first row reads `© UNESCO` and points to:

"Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 IGO"

and its second row reads `non © UNESCO`, listing nomination files and operational guidelines under separate terms.

WHY THE PAGE DOES NOT SETTLE IT. Everything turns on whether a State Party's tentative-list submission is `© UNESCO` content, and the site says two things that pull in opposite directions. The record page's own footer asserts `© UNESCO World Heritage Centre 1992-2026`. The same page's disclaimer says `The sole responsibility for the content of each Tentative List lies with the State Party concerned.` Responsibility is not ownership and the disclaimer does not claim it is, but a text whose sole responsible author is named as somebody other than UNESCO is not obviously UNESCO's own content either, and the terms table's `non © UNESCO` row exists precisely for material in that position without naming tentative lists in it.

WHAT THIS RECORD BELIEVES AND SAYS SO. The safer of the two readings governs here: this record treats its excerpt as covered by the blanket restriction and not by the CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO licence, quotes 1,103 characters of it for research under ruling 74's `COUNTED, NOT GATED` column, and does not assert that the licence reaches it.

THE SHAPE `eastasia-08-songshi-fulin` NAMED AND COULD NOT EXPRESS, ARRIVING FOR THE SECOND TIME. There the source text and the translation came from two sources with two positions and the cell covered one of them and said so. Here one text has two positions asserted over it by one publisher, and the cell records both rather than choosing the flattering one.
notes:
F7's second Southeast Asia `catalogue_record` slot. Fifth record of the tranche, fifty-second in the corpus.

THE DUPLICATION WITH `seasia-02-oc-eo-site` IS DELIBERATE AND WAS DECLARED IN `F7_CURATION_START.md` BEFORE THIS RECORD EXISTED. Óc Eo is already in this corpus twice — the Antoninus Pius medallion and a site summary — and nobody re-curates a record, so both stay. What this adds is a DIFFERENT GENRE OF WITNESS for the same site. `seasia-02-oc-eo-site` cites Wikipedia. This is a nomination dossier's summary, filed by a national commission with a State Party's name on it and a reference number, and it says in the State Party's own words that Roman gold coins and medals were found there.

AND IT IS THE CLEANEST SUBJECT-CROWDING EXPERIMENT F7 CAN RUN — RULING 79's P2. `au-oc-eo-medallion` sits at rank 1 expecting `seasia-01-oc-eo-medallion`, and this record is English prose naming the same site, the same excavation and the same class of object, in the same language as the target's own description. F6's P4 could not run this experiment: `au-ezana-titles` held rank 1 against four new records, and the record P4 was about resembled it only regionally. P2 predicts this pair leaves rank 1 and that chunks of this record are in its `beaten_by`. If it holds with an empty `beaten_by`, resemblance does not reach the top of the list, and that is worth as much as the record.

WHAT THE SENTENCE ACTUALLY SAYS, AND WHY IT IS BETTER THAN A CATALOGUE ENTRY. `International trade has been proven through artifacts found such as wooden boat pieces, copper Roman gold coins and medals, Han bronze mirrors, Persian lamps; glass materials, precious metals imported from India and Mediterranean countries`. Rome, Han China and Persia in one clause, as three of the places whose goods turned up in one Mekong Delta town — which is Mundus Ulterior's premise stated by a government describing its own archaeology, rather than by this project arranging records side by side. `seasia-01-oc-eo-medallion` holds ONE of those objects; this holds the sentence that puts it in company.

THE PARAGRAPH IS QUOTED WHOLE AND THAT IS A DECISION. Everything before the trade sentence is stilt houses, canals, boats and cooking pots — the domestic life the submission is arguing for under criterion (v). Cutting to the imports would have made the source look like a list of Roman finds, which is what this corpus would like it to be and not what it is.

COORDINATES WERE ON OFFER AND WERE REFUSED, for the third time in this tranche. The page prints `N100 15 24 E105 08 36`; the latitude's degrees field is evidently mistyped and the corpus would have refused a correct one on the same rule.
